why-particle-size-changes-everything-in-: Why Particle Size Matters in a Root Bark Dye Pot
Milling adds no color to bark. It multiplies the surface where color crosses into water, which is why powder works faster, strains harder and spoils sooner.
what-tannins-do-in-a-dye-bath: What Tannins Do in a Natural Dye Bath
Tannins bind to protein and to metal ions. That is why tannin-rich bark takes strongly on wool and silk, needs help on cotton, and darkens with a pinch of iron.
testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece: Testing a Natural Dye Before You Commit a Fleece
Ten grams of yarn answers in an afternoon what a whole fleece answers in a ruined week. Dye small skeins from one bath and change one thing at a time.
storing-root-bark-so-it-lasts: How to Store Mimosa Hostilis Root Bark So It Lasts
Root bark does not expire on a date. Damp, heat and light spoil it, in that order. Kept sealed, dry, dark and at an even temperature, it holds color for years.
mordanting-wool-before-a-bark-bath: Mordanting Wool With Alum Before a Root Bark Dye Bath
Mordant wool with alum at ten to fifteen per cent of the dry fibre weight, fully dissolved, held just under a simmer for an hour, then left to cool in the pot.
keeping-a-bark-bath-purple: Keeping a Mimosa Hostilis Dye Bath Purple, Not Brown
Brown is what heat does to this color. Hold the bath near eighty degrees, soak the bark cold overnight first, and strain it out before the fibre goes in.
filtering-a-bark-bath-without-losing-the: Filtering a Bark Dye Bath Without Losing the Color
Fine bark particles do not settle. Hold the material in a mesh bag from the start, or pour the bath through doubled muslin, and filter warm, never boiling.
dyeing-leather-with-bark: Dyeing Vegetable-Tanned Leather With Root Bark
Vegetable-tanned leather takes a bark solution readily. Use a strong, well-strained liquid, build color in thin coats, and let each coat dry before judging it.
weighing-bark-against-fibre: How Much Root Bark Per Pound of Fibre for Dyeing
Start at fifty to a hundred per cent of the dry fibre weight, half a pound of bark to a pound of wool for a mid shade, a pound to a pound for a deep one.
iron-as-a-modifier-how-far-to-go: Iron as a Dye Modifier, and How Far to Go
Iron darkens and greys a tannin color in seconds, purple to slate and brown to charcoal. Keep it to one or two per cent of fibre weight and dip, do not simmer.
getting-a-second-and-third-bath-from-one: Getting a Second and Third Dye Bath From One Batch
Spent bark still holds color. A second bath gives a shade or two lighter and a third lighter again. Keep the bark wet between baths and use it within days.
wool-silk-cotton-and-linen-in-the-same-b: Wool, Silk, Cotton and Linen in the Same Dye Bath
Wool and silk go deep with alum alone. Cotton and linen need a tannin step and two alum baths and still land paler, so dyeing them together disappoints one.
cold-soak-or-straight-to-heat: Cold Soak or Straight to Heat for a Bark Dye Bath
A cold overnight soak pulls a great deal of color out before any heat is applied, so the pot needs less time hot and is far less likely to brown.
the-faults-that-spoil-a-first-bath: Eight Faults That Spoil a First Natural Dye Bath
Most disappointing first baths come down to eight faults, such as boiling, skipping the scour, undissolved alum and weighing wet fibre. All are cheap to fix.
does-the-colour-last-testing-light-and-w: Does Natural Dye Last? Light and Wash Tests at Home
Two home tests answer it. Tape half a dyed sample in a south-facing window for four weeks, and wash another four times beside a white swatch.
bark-as-a-colourant-in-cold-process-soap: Root Bark as a Colorant in Cold Process Soap
Soap is alkaline, which pushes a tannin color towards tan, khaki and brown. Use one to two teaspoons of fine powder per pound of oils, added at a light trace.
a-plain-glossary-of-natural-dyeing-terms: A Plain Glossary of Natural Dyeing Terms
Mordant, scour, WOF, exhaust bath, modifier, fastness, tannin. Twenty terms cover nearly every natural dyeing instruction, and each is explained here plainly.
buying-by-the-pound-and-what-it-saves: Buying Root Bark by the Pound, and How Far It Goes
A pound of root bark dyes roughly one to two pounds of wool at useful depth, more with exhaust baths, and one larger batch keeps color consistent across a run.
working-safely-with-fine-milled-bark: Working Safely With Fine Milled Root Bark Powder
Fine milled bark makes a dust that irritates eyes, nose and airways. Open the bag in still air, wear a fitted N95 or P2 mask, and wipe surfaces damp.
sassafras-albidum-the-north-american-dye: Sassafras Albidum, a North American Dye Tree
Sassafras albidum is a small tree of eastern North America with three leaf shapes on one branch. Dyers use its root bark for rose-tan and orange-brown shades.
milling-your-own-powder-at-home: Milling Your Own Powder From Shredded Root Bark
A coffee or spice grinder takes shredded bark to a usable powder in short bursts, sieved between passes. Worth doing for small amounts, not for volume.
what-a-batch-code-is-for: What a Batch Code on a Bag of Root Bark Is For
A batch code ties a bag of root bark to one harvest, one milling run and one set of paperwork, and explains why two bags of the same cut can dye differently.
what-iso-17025-accreditation-means: What ISO/IEC 17025 Accreditation Means for a Testing Lab
ISO/IEC 17025 is the international standard for testing lab competence. Accreditation covers only the tests on a lab's scope, so check the scope, not the logo.
what-a-contaminant-panel-actually-covers: What a Contaminant Panel Actually Covers for Dried Bark
A contaminant panel for dried bark usually checks lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury, microbial counts, pesticide residues, moisture and foreign matter.
why-a-test-date-matters-as-much-as-the-f: Why a Lab Test Date Matters as Much as the Figure
Dried bark keeps changing after it is tested. Moisture drifts, light fades the surface and air oxidizes tannins, so a report describes the day it was sampled.
a-glossary-of-certificate-terms: A Glossary of Certificate of Analysis Terms for Botanicals
LOD and LOQ set what a method can see and measure, ND means nothing found above that level, ppm and ppb express tiny amounts, and CFU per gram counts microbes.
the-three-cuts-of-mimosa-root-bark: The Three Cuts of Mimosa Root Bark, and Who Each One Suits
Powder, shredded bark and stripped root are one material cut three ways. Powder gives color fastest, shredded suits most dyers, and stripped root keeps longest.
using-ph-to-steer-the-shade: Using pH to Steer the Shade of a Root Bark Dye
A small pH shift moves this color a long way. Acid pushes it towards red and rust, alkali towards violet and grey. Keep wool between pH 5 and 8.
is-mimosa-hostilis-dye-colorfast: Is Mimosa Hostilis Dye Colorfast on Wool and Silk?
On wool and silk, Mimosa hostilis gives colors that hold well in the wash and reasonably well in light, because its tannins bind to protein fiber.
eco-printing-silk-with-mimosa-hostilis: Eco Printing Silk With Mimosa Hostilis Root Bark
To eco print silk with Mimosa hostilis, dye the silk in a bark bath, lay mordanted leaves on it, roll it tightly around a dowel and steam for about an hour.
mimosa-hostilis-vs-cutch-oak-gall-and-qu: Mimosa Hostilis Compared With Cutch, Oak Gall and Quebracho
Mimosa hostilis, cutch, oak gall and quebracho are all tannin dyes but not interchangeable. Mimosa gives rose, plum and burgundy, cutch gives warm browns.
reading-a-label-line-by-line: Reading a Root Bark Label Line by Line
A root bark label should give the botanical name, the part and cut, the net weight, a batch code and a clear not for human consumption statement.
